input: A continuous stirred-tank reactor, or CSTR, is used to carry out a neutralisation reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant, and the performance of the reactor under steady-state conditions can be estimated in a fairly straightforward manner from the kinetic and operating data available. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.282 min-1, and the mean residence time of the material in the vessel is 85 min, so that the product of the rate constant and the residence time comes to 23.97, a comfortably large value that already suggests a high degree of conversion. Applying the standard design relation for an ideal CSTR under these conditions gives a steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant of 96%, which is to say that only a small residual fraction of the limiting reactant leaves the reactor unreacted in the effluent stream. It is, however, important to appreciate that this estimate is built upon some significant idealising assumptions, most notably the assumptions of perfect mixing throughout the vessel contents and of constant density across the reactor, and in a real vessel there may well be dead zones, short-circuiting or incomplete dispersion that cause the actual behaviour to depart from the ideal picture. Compounding this uncertainty, tracer tests on the actual vessel, which would reveal the true residence time distribution, have not in fact been run, so the closeness of the real reactor to the ideal model remains unverified. The 96% conversion should consequently be interpreted as an ideal-model estimate representing something close to an upper bound on performance, rather than as a guaranteed operating result, and the true conversion achieved in practice may fall somewhat below this figure if the mixing in the actual vessel turns out to be imperfect.
target: Steady-state conversion for an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) running a first-order neutralisation is 96% of the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.282 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 85 min; the product of rate constant and residence time is 23.97, and the ideal-CSTR conversion relation applied to that product gives the stated conversion. A product well above unity is what the conversion rests on: at a product near one, the same relation returns a conversion near one half, and the estimate would be far more sensitive to errors in either input. Two assumptions carry the result. Mixing is taken as perfect, so the whole vessel contents sit at the effluent composition and the reaction proceeds everywhere at the exit rate; density is taken as constant, so the residence time computed from volume and feed rate is the residence time the reacting material experiences. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual vessel. Tracer tests, which would return the residence time distribution and expose dead volume or short-circuiting, have not been run. Dead volume lowers the effective residence time below the stated value, short-circuiting lets part of the feed leave early, and each defect lowers the conversion below the ideal value. The 96% figure is therefore an ideal-model estimate and an upper bound for the stated kinetics, not a measured performance. It is adequate for comparing operating conditions on a common basis, and for sizing downstream equipment that must handle the unreacted remainder; a guarantee of effluent quality would need the tracer response of the actual vessel.
